title: I read 55 flight-deal-finder repos made since Amadeus shut down. 26 of them now call SerpApi
author: Hugues Ishema
summary: TL;DR: Amadeus Self-Service closed on 17 July 2026. Kiwi's Tequila API has taken new partners by invitation only since May 2024. So what do people building a "flight deal finder" use now? I cloned all 55 public GitHub repos with that name created since 17 July and checked which flight API their code actually calls. 26 of the 43 that fetch live prices call SerpApi, and the ones that mention a plan build around its free 250 searches a month. Three still call test.api.amadeus.com , a hostname that no longer resolves. Below: the numbers, what 250 searches buys you, and a 20-line replacement I ran on 26 November 2026. Why this keeps coming up "Flight deal finder" is a classic Python project. It's the Day 39–40 capstone of a very popular Python course: keep destinations and target prices in a Google Sheet, check fares, send an alert when one drops below target. It's also what a lot of people build for themselves. The project needs a free flight API, and those have been closing: API Status (checked 26 Nov 2026) Amadeus Self-Service Shut down 17 July 2026. test.api.amadeus.com returns no DNS record Kiwi.com Tequila "Any new partnerships on the Tequila platform will be on an invitation only basis" ( Kiwi.com, 30 May 2024 ) Skyscanner Commercial agreement only; an account manager contacts you ( Skyscanner partner help ) Google QPX Express Closed April 2018 What 55 new repos actually use Method: GitHub search for "flight deal finder" with created:>2026-07-17 returned 55 repos on 26 November 2026. I shallow-cloned all of them and searched the code (not the READMEs) for each provider's host or client library, then opened the leftovers by hand. A repo can count under more than one source. The 25 that mention Sheety, "100 Days" or "Day 39/40" are counted as course projects. Data source in the code Repos Course projects SerpApi (Google Flights engine) 26 19 Travelpayouts / Aviasales 6 0 Scrapes a site itself (Playwright, Selenium, or plain requests) 6 1 Amadeus 5 3 fast-flights / fli (Google Flights, unofficial) 3 0 Duffel 1 0 Kiwi Tequila 1 0 seats.aero (award seats) 1 0 Endpoint hidden in an env var 2 2 No live data (mock data, UI template, empty repo) 12 0 Three things stood out: SerpApi is the new default. 26 of the 43 repos with live data use it, including 19 of the 25 course projects. The free tier is the design constraint. READMEs say it plainly: one caches responses "to not use up SerpAPI calls during testing as there is a 250 call limit", another never goes below 25 remaining searches and caps itself at 10 per run. Copied Amadeus code is dead code. All three course repos that call Amadeus use https://test.api.amadeus.com/v1/security/oauth2/token . They were created in August and October 2026, after the shutdown. That host has no DNS record now, so the first request fails before it reaches any server. The repo list and per-repo labels are in the study folder . What 250 searches a month buys you One search is one route on one date. The course-style job of watching 5 destinations and checking the next 8 departure days for each is 40 searches. Once a day, that's about 1,200 a month. Option Price (checked 26 Nov 2026) 40 searches a day for 30 days SerpApi Free 250 searches/month Runs out on day 7 SerpApi Starter $25/month for 1,000 searches Runs out on day 26 Google Flights Scraper on Apify (below) $0.003 per search + $0.0005 per flight saved $4.20, inside Apify's $5/month free usage SerpApi returns more per search than my setup below, with full itineraries and booking options. If you need those, the comparison changes. For "tell me when it's cheap", you need one number per route and date. One more thing READMEs mention: Google sued SerpApi in December 2025 over scraping. My tool also reads Google Flights pages, so the same uncertainty applies to it. Store the prices you collect, and you keep your history whatever happens to any provider. A replacement for check_flights() This keeps the course's idea (destinations plus a target price) and swaps the API call. It runs on Apify with apify-client 3.x: import os from apify_client import ApifyClient # What the course keeps in a Google Sheet: destination and the price that counts as a deal targets = { "CDG" : 60 , "FRA" : 60 , "IST" : 90 , "JFK" : 300 , "HND" : 600 } # GBP, one-way client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ "APIFY_TOKEN" ] ) run = client . actor ( "kuezi/google-flights-scraper" ) . call ( logger = None , run_input = { "routes" : [ f "LHR-{iata}" for iata in targets ] , "departureDate" : "2027-01-11" , "scanDays" : 7 , # 11 Jan plus the next 7 days "maxFlightsPerSearch" : 1 , # we only want the price, not 30 itineraries "currency" : "GBP" , "country" : "gb" , } ) summary = client . key_value_store ( run . default_key_value_store_id ) . get_record ( "SUMMARY" ) [ "value" ] for r in summary [ "cheapestByRoute" ] : to = r [ "route" ] . split ( "-" ) [ 1 ] flag = "DEAL" if r [ "cheapestPrice" ] <= targets [ to ] else " " print ( f '{flag} {r["route"]}: £{r["cheapestPrice"]} on {r["cheapestDates"][0]} ' f '(median £{r["medianPrice"]}, {r["daysScanned"]} days)' ) print ( len ( summary [ "searches" ] ) , "searches," , run . status ) Real output (26 November 2026, 36 seconds): LHR-CDG: £68 on 2027-01-11 (median £68, 8 days) LHR-FRA: £70 on 2027-01-11 (median £70, 8 days) DEAL LHR-HND: £478 on 2027-01-12 (median £478, 8 days) LHR-IST: £96 on 2027-01-12 (median £96, 8 days) DEAL LHR-JFK: £279 on 2027-01-13 (median £316, 8 days) 40 searches, SUCCEEDED cheapestPrice is the lowest fare across everything Google listed for that day, even though only one flight per day is saved. Each saved flight carries the airline, times, stops and a Google Flights link you can put in the alert email. Swap the print for your email or Telegram call and schedule it on Apify or in cron. Google Flights Scraper on Apify . Disclosure: I built this. This run was 40 searches and 40 saved flights, so $0.14 at the free-plan price. Empty and failed searches are free. If your code was written for Amadeus's response shape, I covered a drop-in for the Flight Offers endpoint earlier. Limits, honestly 55 repos is a snapshot, not a census. Many projects aren't named "flight deal finder", and private ones don't show up. I classified repos by code search, so a provider called through an env-var URL can be missed. I found two of those and listed them as unclear. Prices move. The fares above are from one run on 26 November 2026. No booking. You get prices and links, not tickets. Unofficial data. Google can change its pages at any time, and every Google Flights tool breaks when it does, mine included. If you're doing the course project and hit something this doesn't cover, say so in the comments. AI disclosure: I wrote this with AI assistance. The repo counts, the DNS check and the run above were done on 26 November 2026.

title: De 15 minutos para 1 minuto: o script que gera os contratos do escritório onde trabalho
author: Gabriel Victor
summary: Trabalho num escritório de advocacia previdenciária desde janeiro e estou no 2º semestre de Engenharia de Software. Todo cliente novo precisa de um contrato, e quase todos passam pela minha mão: são de 10 a 15 por semana. Fazer um contrato à mão levava uns 15 minutos. Abrir o modelo no Word, trocar nome, CPF, endereço e benefício, conferir tudo e mandar imprimir. Parece pouco, mas são de duas horas e meia a quase quatro horas por semana fazendo a mesma coisa, e cada digitação é uma chance de errar um número de CPF. Hoje o mesmo contrato sai em cerca de 1 minuto. Vou contar como cheguei nisso, incluindo o que deu errado no caminho. A primeira tentativa: deixar a IA fazer tudo Minha primeira ideia foi pedir para a IA editar os documentos direto. Funcionou mais ou menos: chegou a levar 20 minutos para 3 documentos, mandou para a impressora errada e uma vez gerou um contrato com um dado faltando. Para um documento que o cliente vai assinar, "mais ou menos" não serve. O que eu aprendi ali: para uma tarefa que se repete sempre igual, um script é melhor do que a IA. O script faz a mesma coisa toda vez. A IA, não. A descoberta que simplificou tudo Quando fui organizar os modelos, achei que eram 11 contratos diferentes, um para cada benefício. Olhando com calma, era um contrato só : o que mudava era o nome do benefício. E os outros documentos do kit (procuração, declarações) usavam o mesmo bloco com os dados do cliente. Isso virou a base do projeto: um modelo, com marcadores no lugar dos dados ( {{NOME}} , {{CPF}} , {{ENDERECO}} , {{BENEFICIO}} ...), e um script que troca cada marcador pelo dado certo. Como montei Eu não escrevi o código sozinho, e não escondo isso. O que fiz foi: Escrever o passo a passo em português, antes de qualquer código: PARA cada contrato novo: ler os dados da ficha do cliente SE faltar um campo obrigatório: avisar o que falta e parar abrir o modelo aprovado pelos advogados trocar cada marcador pelo dado salvar na pasta do cliente mandar para a impressora certa Usar o Claude Code para transformar esse passo a passo num script em Python. Testar com casos reais, conferindo campo por campo. Achar os erros e pedir as correções até o resultado sair igual todas as vezes. A IA continua no processo, mas só numa parte: ela me ajuda a reunir os dados da ficha. O texto do contrato vem sempre do modelo que os advogados aprovaram, nunca da IA. Os detalhes que deram trabalho Masculino e feminino. O contrato diz "inscrito" ou "inscrita", "domiciliado" ou "domiciliada". O script descobre pelo estado civil informado na ficha (viúvo ou viúva, casado ou casada). Campo faltando. Antes de gerar, o script confere se todos os campos obrigatórios estão preenchidos. Se falta algum, ele para e avisa, em vez de gerar um contrato pela metade. Outro computador. Levei o sistema para outra máquina sem padronizar nada antes, e lá o resultado saiu diferente. Hoje eu padronizo tudo primeiro. E todo contrato ainda passa por uma pessoa antes de ser assinado. O resultado Antes Depois Tempo por contrato ~15 minutos ~1 minuto Contratos por semana 10 a 15 10 a 15 Tempo por semana 2h30 a 3h45 10 a 15 minutos Quer ver funcionando? O código e os modelos do escritório não podem ser públicos, porque envolvem dados de clientes. Então fiz uma demonstração com um modelo e um cliente fictícios, que roda direto no navegador e segue o mesmo caminho: ler a ficha, conferir os campos, abrir o modelo, trocar os marcadores e entregar o contrato. 👉 Testar a demonstração O que eu levo disso Antes de pensar em ferramenta, vale olhar para o problema com calma. A descoberta de que eram um contrato só, e não onze, poupou mais trabalho do que qualquer linha de código. E usar IA para programar não tira a responsabilidade de quem publica: sou eu que testo, acho os erros e respondo pelo resultado. Se você também trabalha num lugar cheio de tarefas repetitivas, comece anotando quanto tempo cada uma leva. É ali que estão os primeiros projetos.

title: Building Coroner with Kiro: Why Docker Exit Code 137 Is Not a Root Cause
author: Prabhakaran Jayaraman Masani
summary: How I built an open-source container crash-forensics tool using Kiro specifications, external telemetry, Docker termination records and property-based testing. Two Python containers terminate with the same exit code: 137 . One was deliberately killed with SIGKILL. The other was killed after Docker recorded an out-of-memory event. If I examined only the exit codes, I would see the same result. Yet the recorded termination mechanisms are different. That observation became the central problem behind Coroner , an open-source crash-forensics tool I built using Kiro for the Kiroween 2026 hackathon . The goal was not to create another dashboard that confidently guesses why a container failed. I wanted to preserve the evidence that existed before the container died, compare independent sources and show where the available information stops supporting a conclusion. The problem: What survives a container crash? When a container terminates unexpectedly, developers often start with a few familiar questions: What was its exit code? Did it run out of memory? What happened immediately before termination? Can the last recorded measurements be trusted? Are we inferring something that the evidence does not establish? Docker's State.ExitCode is useful, but it is not a complete diagnosis. Exit code 137 commonly indicates termination by SIGKILL. It does not, by itself, establish an out-of-memory kill. Another problem is evidence survival. If telemetry is stored only inside a container that terminates, the information needed for investigation may be lost with the container. Coroner addresses these issues by preserving acknowledged samples outside the application container and examining them alongside Docker's termination records. Building the architecture Coroner has four components. Component Responsibility Probe Runs inside the Python application container and captures process samples, including RSS Collector Receives samples and stores acknowledged evidence outside the failing container Runner Executes controlled termination experiments and records Docker state Viewer Reads preserved evidence and presents timelines, recorded values and comparisons The Probe samples process information every 500 milliseconds by default. The Collector stores acknowledged samples as JSON Lines evidence on a separate Docker volume. The design distinguishes delivered samples from samples that could not be delivered. The Runner controls the experiments and collects Docker termination details, including ExitCode , OOMKilled and the run manifest. Finally, the Viewer displays the preserved evidence through a local, read-only web interface. The Viewer starts no containers and does not modify saved runs. That distinction matters. Reviewing evidence should not itself reproduce a destructive experiment. Three experiments, one important difference I created three controlled experiments using Docker Desktop with Linux containers on a Windows development machine. The recorded results were: Experiment ExitCode OOMKilled Preserved samples A — Controlled fatal exit 1 false 15 B — Runner sends SIGKILL 137 false 15 C — Docker OOM kill 137 true 45 Experiment A establishes a controlled fatal process exit. Experiment B terminates after the Runner issues docker kill --signal=KILL . Docker records exit code 137 and OOMKilled: false . Experiment C also returns exit code 137, but Docker records OOMKilled: true under a 128 MiB memory limit. The highest preserved RSS sample in C was 141,090,816 bytes, approximately 134.55 MiB. The sampled RSS and the cgroup memory accounting that triggers an OOM kill are different measurements. Coroner does not treat a high RSS sample alone as proof of why the kernel terminated the container. The important evidence is the Docker termination record, considered alongside the Runner's actions and preserved samples. The Viewer's comparison page states the result: The same exit code does not always mean the same failure. This is the central demonstration in the project. A second problem: Clocks do not automatically agree Building the timeline exposed another issue. The Probe, Collector, Runner and Docker records have different timestamp sources. A timestamp without its clock provenance can make an investigation appear more certain than it actually is. For Experiment B, the Runner recorded one timestamp immediately before issuing the kill command and another after the command returned. Those recorded timestamps were 425 milliseconds apart. That interval does not establish when the SIGKILL signal reached the container. Coroner's Viewer uses a derived host-equivalent axis for B's memory samples. The derivation is labelled and is not independently verified as clock synchronisation. Experiments A and C retain raw Probe capture time. The design decision was straightforward: show the clock source, label derived timing information and avoid inventing an ordering that the evidence cannot prove. How Kiro shaped the development process I used Kiro's spec-driven development workflow to organise Coroner rather than treating the project as one large coding task. The repository contains three specifications. M0 — Evidence pipeline This milestone established the requirements and design for the Probe, Collector, Runner and controlled experiments. M1 — Forensic Viewer This milestone organised the read-only interface, evidence presentation, timing information and comparison behaviour. M2 — Demonstration and verification This milestone documented judge instructions, reproducibility checks, safety constraints and recording tasks. For M0 and M1, the Kiro specifications contain: requirements.md — What the system must do. design.md — Architecture and technical decisions. tasks.md — Development tasks, verification steps and checkpoints. tasks.meta.json — Recorded task execution history. The development tasks reference requirements and include verification commands, expected behaviour and safety constraints. Checkpoints require actual test results before work is accepted. Kiro's task execution history is preserved in tasks.meta.json . I treat those records as evidence of development activity, not proof of correctness. The tests and acceptance reports provide the separate verification. You can inspect the actual Kiro files: https://github.com/prabhakaran-jm/coroner/tree/master/.kiro/specs Property-based testing uncovered real defects One of the most useful parts of the development process involved Hypothesis , the Python property-based testing library. Instead of testing only selected examples, property-based tests generate many inputs and explore behaviours that are easy to overlook. Coroner includes 28 test_prop_* files containing 83 Hypothesis @given tests. The properties cover areas such as: Sample sequencing and missing-data accounting. Evidence durability and recovery. Dropped-sample handling. Collector acknowledgement behaviour. Runner verdict and manifest consistency. The Collector's storage-status probe produced two particularly useful findings. Defect 1: A later error could hide an earlier failure If fsync failed and closing the file also failed, the close error could replace the more important earlier failure. A property-test counterexample exposed this behaviour. The fix explicitly retained the earlier failure rather than allowing a later close error to mask it. Defect 2: Exception messages could contain control characters Generated exception messages demonstrated that non-printable characters could reach the storage-status error text. The fix replaced those characters with safe printable placeholders. These findings matter because Coroner's purpose depends on evidence being recorded and reported accurately. A forensic tool should not quietly misrepresent a storage failure. Verification results The recorded full unit-test run used a clean Windows checkout with Python 3.12.10. Result Count Collected 5,995 Passed 5,982 Failed 0 Skipped 13 Process exit code 0 The skipped tests include platform-specific checks, a Node-dependent test and tests requiring the unpublished real run files. The Viewer has also been exercised through automated headless-Chrome checks. This does not establish that every platform, browser or accessibility scenario has been tested. The real Docker experiments were verified on one Windows host using Docker Desktop. Native Linux and macOS have not been verified. A reproducible demonstration without Docker I wanted other developers and hackathon judges to inspect the Viewer without having to run destructive container experiments. The public repository includes scripts/make-sample-runs.py . It generates three clearly labelled synthetic runs carrying the same key ExitCode and OOMKilled values as the recorded demonstration. These synthetic files are not real container measurements and do not reproduce the Docker experiments. They provide a safe way to exercise the Viewer and its comparison behaviour. The complete setup instructions are available in JUDGING.md . What I learned Building Coroner reinforced three engineering lessons. First, preserving information is not the same as understanding its cause. An exit code is a recorded fact. A root-cause explanation requires further evidence. Second, an accurate interface must distinguish recorded facts from derived values and missing observations. A graph becomes more useful when the viewer knows which timestamps are measured, which are derived and what remains unknown. Third, tests and development records serve different purposes. A completed task shows development progress. A verified test provides evidence about a particular behaviour under particular conditions. Kiro's specification workflow helped keep those distinctions visible throughout the project. The most useful outcome was not a larger codebase. It was a tool with clearer boundaries around what its evidence can establish. What comes next? Coroner is an open-source foundation for further container failure investigation. Possible next steps include: Testing on native Linux hosts and macOS. Supporting more container termination scenarios. Improving the presentation of timing uncertainty. Expanding human usability and accessibility testing. Making saved evidence easier to share and examine across environments. I also want to explore how developer tools can communicate uncertainty without making the user work harder. Explore Coroner Coroner is open source under the MIT licence. GitHub repository: https://github.com/prabhakaran-jm/coroner Demo video — Kiroween 2026: https://youtu.be/V1TVWcnrygg Run Coroner locally: https://github.com/prabhakaran-jm/coroner/blob/master/JUDGING.md Kiro specifications: https://github.com/prabhakaran-jm/coroner/tree/master/.kiro/specs This article was written as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon, where I built Coroner using Kiro's spec-driven development workflow. If you were investigating a production container crash, which evidence would you trust first, and what would you refuse to conclude without further measurements?

title: Computing ANSI Z765-2021 Heated GLA, 16" OC Framing & 4x8 Drywall Takeoffs from a 2D Wall Graph in TypeScript
author: Clara Sutton
summary: If you sum the interior areas of every room in a 2D floor plan and call the result "square footage," your number will disagree with a US residential appraiser by 6% to 10% on almost every house. When we built the geometry kernel for PlanCaliber (a browser-based 2D/3D CAD and floor plan studio), we ran straight into three real-world measurement rules that naive room-area calculators get wrong: ANSI Z765-2021 Gross Living Area (GLA) is measured out-to-out along exterior finished surfaces (including interior wall thickness), while excluding garages, porches, decks, and enclosed unheated voids. 16" O.C. Wood Stud Framing is never just linearFeet / 1.333 : wall ends, corners, double top plates, single bottom plates, and king/jack/cripple framing around doors and windows typically add 30% to 45% more lumber. 4x8 Gypsum Drywall & Baseboard Takeoffs depend on wall topology: exterior walls receive drywall on one side and deduct exterior door widths once, while interior partitions receive drywall on two sides and deduct interior passage doors twice. Here is how we compute all three deterministically in pure TypeScript directly from a planar centerline wall graph, with zero native C++ geometry kernels. 1. Reconstructing Out-to-Out ANSI Z765-2021 Heated GLA from Centerline Polygons In a planar floor plan engine, walls are stored as centerline segments connecting vertices, and rooms are detected as minimal closed cycles of half-edges. That representation gives you two clean properties: Every interior partition shared by two heated rooms sits inside the union of their centerline room cycles (half its thickness is inside room A's centerline cycle, half is inside room B's centerline cycle). Every exterior wall (or demising wall bordering an unheated garage) is touched by only one heated room cycle ( count === 1 ), meaning the outer thicknessIn / 2 strip lies outside the centerline loop. Instead of running an expensive Minkowski polygon offset on every drag frame (60 FPS in a browser), we compute the exact ANSI out-to-out area in $O(V + E)$ time by tracking wall incidence counts ( glaCountByWall ) and parent-child polygon containment ( parentIdx ): // 1. Start with top-level heated room centerline cycles (includes interior partitions automatically) let glaSqIn = 0 ; for ( const i of topGlaIndices ) { glaSqIn += rooms [ i ] . grossCycleSqFt * 144 ; } // 2. Subtract any enclosed non-GLA void (e.g., an interior courtyard or garage island) for ( let i = 0 ; i < rooms . length ; i ++ ) { const p = parentIdx [ i ] ; if ( ! rooms [ i ] . includeInGla && p !== - 1 && rooms [ p ] . includeInGla ) { glaSqIn = Math . max ( 0 , glaSqIn - rooms [ i ] . grossCycleSqFt * 144 ) ; } } // 3. Add the outer half-wall strip on every perimeter or garage-demising wall let glaExtPerimeterCount = 0 ; let avgExtHalfT = 3 ; // 6" exterior wall -> 3" half-thickness default for ( const [ wid , count ] of glaCountByWall . entries ( ) ) { const sw = wallMap . get ( wid ) ; if ( ! sw ) continue ; if ( count === 1 ) { const halfT = sw . wall . thicknessIn / 2 ; glaSqIn += sw . lengthIn * halfT ; glaExtPerimeterCount += 1 ; avgExtHalfT = halfT ; } } // 4. Close the 4 convex outer corner squares (halfT x halfT each) if ( glaExtPerimeterCount >= 4 ) { glaSqIn += 4 * avgExtHalfT * avgExtHalfT ; } const heatedGlaSqFt = Number ( ( glaSqIn / 144 ) . toFixed ( 1 ) ) ; Sanity check on a 36'-0" x 28'-0" rectangular house Suppose exterior walls are 6" thick ( halfT = 3" ), so centerlines span 35'-6" (426") by 27'-6" (330"): Centerline cycle area: 426 x 330 = 140,580 sq in ( 976.25 sq ft ) Four outer half-wall strips: 2 * (426 + 330) * 3 = 4,536 sq in ( 31.50 sq ft ) Four outer corner squares: 4 * (3 x 3) = 36 sq in ( 0.25 sq ft ) Total out-to-out GLA: 976.25 + 31.50 + 0.25 = 1,008.0 sq ft = exact 36 x 28 ! If you attach a 22' x 20' garage along one side, the garage cycle has includeInGla = false . The demising wall between the kitchen and garage still has glaCountByWall.get(wid) === 1 , so the heated envelope automatically closes cleanly along the house side while nonGlaSqFt tracks the garage separately without double-counting the shared wall. You can test the exact ANSI Z765-2021 calculation (including sloped 5-foot ceiling knee walls and finished below-grade basement separation) interactively in our free ANSI Z765 GLA Square Footage Calculator . 2. 16" O.C. Framing Studs, Plates, and Opening Framing from Hosted Wall Geometry Once walls and hosted openings ( doors , windows , cased_openings ) are solved on the graph, preliminary material takeoff becomes a single deterministic pass over every wall segment. For each solved wall sw of length lengthIn (in inches) and height wallH : Common studs at 16" O.C. : Math.ceil(sw.lengthIn / 16) + 1 End / corner backing : +2 studs per wall run Opening framing : +3 studs per hosted door or window (accounting for king, jack, and cripple equivalents) Top & bottom plate equivalents : residential stud walls use a single bottom plate plus a double top plate ( 3 x lengthIn linear inches), converted to 8-foot ( 96" ) lumber equivalents via Math.ceil((sw.lengthIn * 3) / 96) for ( const sw of walls ) { const wallH = sw . wall . heightIn ?? doc . ceilingHeightIn ?? 108 ; const hosted = doc . openings . filter ( ( o ) => o . wallId === sw . wall . id ) ; const commonStuds = Math . ceil ( sw . lengthIn / 16 ) + 1 ; const openingFraming = hosted . length * 3 ; const plateEquiv = Math . ceil ( ( sw . lengthIn * 3 ) / 96 ) ; studsCount += commonStuds + 2 + openingFraming + plateEquiv ; const grossWallSqFt = ( sw . lengthIn * wallH ) / 144 ; const openingSqFt = hosted . reduce ( ( sum , o ) => sum + ( o . widthIn * Math . max ( 0 , o . headHeightIn - o . sillHeightIn ) ) / 144 , 0 ) ; const netOneSideSqFt = Math . max ( 0 , grossWallSqFt - openingSqFt ) ; if ( sw . wall . kind === 'exterior' ) { extInches += sw . lengthIn ; drywallSqFtRaw += netOneSideSqFt ; // Inside face only } else { intInches += sw . lengthIn ; drywallSqFtRaw += netOneSideSqFt * 2 ; // Both faces } } Ceilings, 4x8 Gypsum Sheets (+10% Waste), and Paint Exterior decks and patios ( roomType === 'deck_patio' ) never receive gypsum ceilings. Every enclosed interior room adds r.areaSqFt to ceilingSqFt , and we apply a standard 10% cut-waste factor before dividing by 32 sq ft per standard 4' x 8' gypsum board: const totalDrywallWithWaste = ( drywallSqFtRaw + ceilingSqFt ) * 1.1 ; const drywallSheets4x8 = Math . max ( 1 , Math . ceil ( totalDrywallWithWaste / 32 ) ) ; // Paint: 2 coats on finished drywall at 350 sq ft per gallon const paintGallons = Math . max ( 1 , Math . ceil ( ( ( drywallSqFtRaw + ceilingSqFt ) * 2 ) / 350 ) ) ; Baseboard Linear Feet with Side-Aware Door Deductions A subtle detail that builders notice immediately: every full-height door or cased opening cuts baseboard trim, but an exterior entry door removes baseboard from one finished wall face while an interior bedroom door removes baseboard from both sides of the partition: let doorDeductFt = 0 ; const wallKindById = new Map ( walls . map ( ( sw ) => [ sw . wall . id , sw . wall . kind ] ) ) ; for ( const op of doc . openings ) { if ( isFullHeightCut ( op ) ) { const sides = wallKindById . get ( op . wallId ) === 'exterior' ? 1 : 2 ; doorDeductFt += ( op . widthIn / 12 ) * sides ; } } // +8% waste for inside/outside miter corners const baseboardLf = Math . max ( 0 , Math . round ( ( rawPerimFt - doorDeductFt ) * 1.08 ) ) ; Try the standalone framing and sheetrock estimator (complete with our visual 16" O.C. wall section reference plate) in the Wall Stud & 4x8 Drywall Takeoff Calculator . 3. Verifying Architectural Paper Scale Fit ( 1/4" = 1'-0" Across US Letter, 11x17, ARCH C & ARCH D) Once GLA and framing takeoffs are calculated, the final step is printing the floor plan at a true architectural scale ( 1/4" = 1'-0" , ratio 1:48 ) without silently shrinking it to fit the printer margins. We model each paper sheet with its exact printable bounding box after subtracting margins and the title block height: export const PAPER_SIZES = [ { id : 'letter' , widthIn : 11 , heightIn : 8.5 , marginIn : 0.5 , titleBlockIn : 0.75 } , { id : 'tabloid' , widthIn : 17 , heightIn : 11 , marginIn : 0.5 , titleBlockIn : 0.90 } , { id : 'arch_c' , widthIn : 24 , heightIn : 18 , marginIn : 0.5 , titleBlockIn : 1.25 } , { id : 'arch_d' , widthIn : 36 , heightIn : 24 , marginIn : 0.5 , titleBlockIn : 1.50 } ] as const ; At 1/4" = 1'-0" ( 0.25 paper inches per real foot): US Letter (8.5" x 11") fits up to roughly 40' x 27' cleanly (ideal for kitchens, bathrooms, garages, and small ADUs). Tabloid / ANSI B (11" x 17") fits up to 64' x 36' (covers most single-story ranch homes and barndominiums). ARCH D (24" x 36") fits up to 140' x 86' at full 1/4" = 1'-0" scale. You can check any building footprint against all four standard US sheet sizes and five architectural scales ( 1/8" through 1/2" = 1'-0" ) in the free Floor Plan Scale & Sheet Size Calculator . Live Demo & Output Note All of these solvers run live in the browser inside PlanCaliber (free to draft in 2D/3D, upload hand sketches or PDFs, and inspect live GLA and clearance checks with no account required; clean unwatermarked PDF/PNG exports are $9 once or $19 once for the full 5-sheet CAD + AutoCAD R12 .DXF + .OBJ + .CSV takeoff pack, no subscription). (All outputs and material counts are preliminary space-planning estimates; verify dimensions, framing details, and local residential code requirements on site before construction.)

title: Валідація ідей через PoC
author: Mike Vasovsky
summary: Клієнт приходить із палаючими очима: «Робимо повноцінний продукт на рік розробки!» Зупиняю це на старті. Замість $50k і пів року хаосу ми пропонуємо PoC (Proof of Concept) за 2 тижні. PoC — це не MVP. Це мінімальний робочий прототип, який перевіряє ТІЛЬКИ одну найскладнішу гіпотезу: чи працює складне API, чи впорається алгоритм із навантаженням. Правила нашого PoC: 1. Жорсткий таймбокс у 10-14 днів. 2. Фокус лише на одному технічному ризику. 3. Результат — чітка відповідь «так» або «ні», а не красивий дизайн. Це заощаджує клієнтам десятки тисяч доларів. Якщо гіпотеза хибна, ми змінюємо архітектуру до того, як спалено бюджет. Більше розборів — у Telegram: t.me/ScriptHub_ukr

title: Why Scheduled Social Media Posts Fail to Publish (and How to Retry Safely)
author: Clienzo
summary: Social media posts fail to publish more often than most schedulers let on. A post sits in the queue marked "scheduled", the time passes, and on one network nothing appears. Sometimes the tool tells you; often it does not, and the first sign is a client asking where Tuesday's post went. This guide sorts the reasons a scheduled post fails into six causes, shows how to tell which one you hit, and gives the fix for each. It also covers the part people get wrong after the fix: retrying without posting twice on the networks that worked. First, find out what actually happened "Failed" is not one state. A post sent to five networks can land on four and be refused by one, and the four that worked must not be touched again. Before you change anything, collect three facts for each network the post was meant for: Did it publish? A link to the live post is the only proof. "Sent" or "scheduled" is not. If not, what did the network say? The error message the network returned, word for word, is the best clue you will get. When? A failure at the scheduled minute points at the post or the account; a failure minutes later, while the network processed a video, points at the media. If your scheduler shows a single status for the whole post, open each network and look. In Clienzo every network on a post shows its own result: a link to the live post, or the reason the network gave. The six causes of a failed post 1. Access expired or was revoked The most common cause. A scheduler publishes with permission the account owner granted, and that permission ends: the owner changed a password, removed the app in the network's settings, lost admin rights on a Page, or a token simply reached its expiry date. Meta, for example, documents that a long-lived user access token lasts about 60 days . How to tell: every post to that one account fails, whatever its content, with a message about permissions, sessions or tokens. Fix: reconnect the account from your scheduler, signing in as someone who still has the right role (Page admin, channel owner). For a client's account, ask the client to reconnect it or to give you the role again. Then check every other post scheduled to that account, because they would all have failed the same way. 2. Media the network will not take Each network has its own rules for images and video: formats, file size, length, aspect ratio, how many images in one post. A video that is fine on YouTube can be too long for a Reel; a post with no image cannot go to Instagram at all. How to tell: the error mentions the media, the format or the size, or the failure comes a few minutes after the scheduled time, once the network has tried to process the file. Fix: check the network's own limits, re-export the file to fit, and give that network its own version of the post if the other networks are fine with the original. One cause that looks like a media problem but is not: the network could not download the file at all. A network fetches your image or video from a URL when it publishes; if that URL has expired or the host blocks the network's crawler, the post fails even though the file is perfect. We hit this ourselves when a robots.txt rule on a file host blocked Meta's fetcher, and Facebook video posts failed until the file was served another way. 3. Text over the network's limit Limits vary from 300 characters on Bluesky to thousands elsewhere, and networks count differently: some count bytes, some count every link as a fixed length. Our guide to character limits by network lists what each one counts. How to tell: the network says the text is too long, or the post fails only on the network with the shortest limit. Fix: shorten that network's version. A scheduler that checks each network's limit as you type catches this before the post is ever scheduled; Clienzo does, for each network a post goes to. 4. The wrong kind of account Some networks only let apps publish from certain accounts. Instagram's publishing API works with professional accounts (business or creator), not personal ones. On Facebook, apps publish to Pages, not to personal profiles. How to tell: the account connected but every post to it fails, or the account never appears as a choice for the post. Fix: switch the account type in the network's settings (for Instagram, to a professional account), then reconnect it. 5. The network had a bad minute Networks have outages, slow responses and rate limits. A post can fail with a generic server error and go through untouched an hour later. Two we have seen in practice: Threads answering "the requested resource does not exist" for a post it had just accepted, a few seconds before the post became available, and Bluesky returning an "UpstreamFailure" from the server that hosts an account. How to tell: the message is vague (server error, timeout, upstream, try again later), the account and media are fine, and other posts to the same network work. Fix: wait, then retry. Do not edit the post first: nothing in it was wrong. 6. The network refused the content Sometimes the network itself declines the post: a link it treats as spam, a duplicate of a post you just made, or content against its rules. How to tell: the message mentions policy, spam, duplicates or a blocked link, and a retry fails the same way. Fix: change what the network objected to (a different link, different wording) rather than retrying the same post. Retry without posting twice Once the cause is fixed, the tempting move is to duplicate the post and schedule it again. If the post went out on some networks, that publishes it twice there, and a client will notice the double before you do. Retry only the networks that failed. In Clienzo, Retry on a partly published post sends to the failed networks and leaves the ones that worked alone. If you reconnected a network with a different account, make sure the retry uses the new connection. Clienzo's Retry swaps in the newest working connection of the same network in that business (Pinterest excepted). If you posted it by hand in the meantime, mark the failure as handled instead of retrying. Common mistakes Trusting "scheduled" as proof a post went out. Rewriting a post that failed because of an outage, then wondering why the next one fails too (the account had expired). Duplicating a partly published post and posting twice on the networks that worked. Fixing one failed post and not checking the other posts scheduled to the same account. Learning about the failure from the client. Doing this in Clienzo Clienzo is built around knowing what happened to a post. Every network on every post shows a link to the live post or the reason it failed. A post that did not go out everywhere moves to the Failed tab with a badge on Posts, you get an alert in the app and an email, and you can have the same alerts in a Discord, Telegram or Slack channel. Retry sends only to the networks that failed, and when an account stops accepting Clienzo you are told before the next post is due. It is on every plan, Free included. More on post delivery tracking . Originally published on the Clienzo blog .

title: How Does a Fancy Text Generator Work Under the Hood?
author: Arlo Bennett
summary: How does a fancy text generator work under the hood? It swaps each plain letter for a different Unicode character that already looks bold, italic, script, or monospace. The Fancy Text Generator does this swap with a simple lookup table. You type normal text, and the tool returns new text made from styled Unicode letters. That swap is the whole trick. There is no font file attached to the output. There is no image hidden in the text. The styled letters are plain text characters, just like A or B. That is why you can paste them into Instagram, WhatsApp, Discord, or a game chat. The app on the other end only needs to support Unicode text. It Is a Character Swap, Not a Font A font changes how a letter looks on screen. It does not change the letter itself. A fancy text generator does the opposite. It changes the letter itself and leaves the font alone. The letter A becomes a different code point that was designed to look bold. The app then draws that new character with its normal font. Think of it like a phone book for letters. The tool holds a table that pairs each plain letter with its styled twin. When you type D, the table returns the bold sans version. When you type r, it returns the bold sans version of r. The tool repeats that step for every letter you type. Spaces and punctuation pass through with little or no change. Here is what that swap looks like in practice. Plain text reads "Dream Big". The Bold Sans style returns "𝗗𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝗕𝗶𝗴". The Monospace style returns "𝙳𝚛𝚎𝚊𝚖 𝙱𝚒𝚐". The Fullwidth style returns "Ｄｒｅａｍ Ｂｉｇ". Each version carries the same words. Each version uses different characters under the surface. That difference matters for developers. A font style is metadata that lives outside the text. A Unicode swap lives inside the text itself. Once the swap is done, the style travels with the string. No style sheet follows it. No app needs to know that a style was applied. The Unicode Block That Makes It Possible Most styled letters come from one Unicode block. The block is called Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols. Its range is U+1D400 to U+1D7FF. That range holds 1,024 code points. It was built for math notation, not for social media bios. Yet it holds exactly what a text styler needs. Inside that block you will find bold serif letters, bold sans letters, italic serif letters, and bold italic letters. You will also find script letters, Fraktur letters, double-struck letters, monospace letters, and plain sans letters. Each set follows the same layout. Uppercase A to Z comes first in each set. Lowercase a to z follows. Digits follow in some sets too. The layout is regular by design. A developer can map plain A to bold A by adding a fixed offset. The same offset logic works for B, C, and the rest of the alphabet. That regularity is why a generator can be built with a small table or a short bit of math. The tool does not need a huge database. It needs one clear rule per style. Here is a concrete case from the live tool. The Bold Serif output for "Dream Big" is "𝐃𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦 𝐁𝐢𝐠". The Script output for the same words is "𝒟𝓇ℯ𝒶𝓂 ℬ𝒾ℊ". Both outputs spell the same phrase. Both come from the same block family. Only the chosen set changes. A developer reading the raw text would see two different strings with the same meaning. One detail deserves care. Not every style in the block is complete in the same way. Script has a few gaps where historic letters are used instead. The tool handles those gaps in its table. A hand-built mapper that assumes a perfect grid will miss those cases. That is why a tested lookup table beats a clever offset formula in production. Why Copy and Paste Works Across Apps Copy and paste works because the clipboard carries characters, not pixels. When you copy styled text, you copy a string of Unicode code points. When you paste it, the target app receives that same string. It does not receive a font name or a style tag. It just draws the characters it was given. That is why the same styled name can show up in a bio, a chat message, and a game lobby. Each app uses its own font to draw the text. Each font includes its own shapes for those Unicode characters. The shapes may differ a little from app to app. The characters stay the same. The system works best when the target font covers the block. Most modern fonts on phones and computers cover the common styled sets. Bold, italic, script, and monospace are widely supported. Some rarer sets may fall back to a different font on an old device. The text still arrives intact. Only the drawing changes. Search and storage work the same way. A database stores the styled string as text. A search box can hold it as text. A screen reader will try to read it as text, though the result may sound odd. The key point stays simple. The style is data, not decoration. It survives the trip because it is part of the string. The Lookup Table in Plain Terms A basic generator needs three parts. First, it needs the input string from the user. Second, it needs a map from plain characters to styled characters. Third, it needs an output step that joins the mapped characters back into one string. That is the core loop. Everything else is interface. The map is the heart of the tool. For Bold Sans, plain D maps to one styled D. Plain r maps to one styled r. The tool walks the input from left to right. It looks up each character in turn. If a character has a styled twin, it uses that twin. If it has no twin, it keeps the plain character. Most tools build one map per style. A tool with 36 styles holds 36 maps. That sounds like a lot of work, yet each map is short. The alphabet has only 26 letters in each case. Digits add ten more slots. A small table can hold the whole set for one style. You can test this idea with a short phrase. Type "Font Generator" into the tool and pick Bold Serif. The tool returns "𝐅𝐨𝐧𝐭 𝐆𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫". Type "Stylish Name" and pick Script. The tool returns "𝒮𝓉𝓎𝓁𝒾𝓈𝒽 𝒩𝒶𝓂ℯ". The words do not change. The code points behind them do. A developer can build the same loop in any language. The steps stay the same in JavaScript, Python, or Go. Read the input. Map each character. Join the result. The hard part is not the loop. The hard part is getting the table right and testing it on real devices. Why It Is Not a Font People often call the output a font. That word is handy, yet it is wrong in a technical sense. A font is a file that tells a system how to draw a character. The styled text from a generator needs no such file. It uses characters that already exist in Unicode. The system draws them with whatever font is active. This distinction explains a common surprise. You paste styled text into an app, and it looks different from the preview. The characters did not change. The font did. The app drew the same code points with its own shapes. A real font change would travel as a setting. A Unicode swap travels as text. The distinction also explains why the style survives a plain text file. Save styled text in a .txt file and reopen it later. The style is still there. Save styled text in a font picker and change the font. The underlying characters stay styled. Fonts affect rendering. Code points affect content. For a developer, this is a useful mental model. Think of the generator as a translator between alphabets. It takes Latin letters and returns styled Latin letters. It does not take a font and apply it. The output is still text, and any text pipeline can carry it. What the Tool Does With Characters Outside the Map Not every character has a styled twin. Numbers, punctuation, and symbols need their own rules. Some styles include styled digits. Some styles leave digits plain. Some styles add marks above or below a letter instead of swapping it. The strikethrough style is a good case. It does not swap letters at all. It adds a combining line after each letter. The output for "Dream Big" is "D̶r̶e̶a̶m̶ B̶i̶g̶". Each base letter stays the same. A combining character follows it and draws a line through it. Underline works the same way with a line below. Wraps work in a different way again. A wrap style adds symbols around the whole phrase. The Stars Wrap output is "★ Dream Big ★". The Hearts Wrap output is "♡ Dream Big ♡". The Crown Wrap output is "👑 Dream Big 👑". The inner words stay plain. Only the frame changes. These edge cases show why a lookup table needs care. A swap style, a combining mark style, and a wrap style need different code paths. A single loop can still handle all three. It just needs to know which path each style uses. A clean design keeps those paths apart so a fix in one style does not break another. Limits and Edge Cases Developers Should Know Styled text is fun, yet it has real limits. The first limit is support. Old systems may lack glyphs for some styled sets. When a glyph is missing, the system shows a box or a question mark. The text is still valid. The display just cannot draw it. The second limit is search. A search engine treats styled letters as different characters from plain letters. A search for plain "Dream Big" will not match "𝗗𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝗕𝗶𝗴" as the same string. That matters if the text needs to be found later. Use styled text for display. Use plain text for search, tags, and file names. The third limit is access. Screen readers may read styled letters by their Unicode names. That can turn a short name into a long, confusing announcement. A bio made only of styled text can be hard to use with assistive tech. Keep plain text nearby for key facts like a name or a link. The fourth limit is length. Some styled characters take more bytes than plain letters. A name that fits in plain text may run long after styling. Social apps with tight limits may cut the styled version short. Test the styled output in the target app before you rely on it. The fifth limit is mixed styles. You can mix two styles in one phrase, yet the result can look messy. Each style has its own weight and spacing. Bold Sans next to Script can clash. One style per phrase keeps the result clean. If you need contrast, change the words, not the style mid-phrase. None of these limits break the tool. They just set where it fits best. Styled text works well for names, short bios, headings, and game tags. It works less well for long posts, legal text, or anything that must be searched. Pick the job that fits the tool. How to Check the Output Before You Use It A quick check saves trouble later. Paste the styled text into the app where it will live. Look at it on a phone and on a desktop if you can. Check that no boxes appear in place of letters. Check that the text still fits the field. Try the decode step too. The Fancy Text Generator can turn styled text back into plain text. That reverse step is a good test. If the tool can read the styled string and return plain "Dream Big", the mapping is clean. If it cannot, the string may hold a mixed set or a stray mark. You can also compare styles side by side. The Fancy Text Examples page shows all 36 styles with the same sample words. That view makes it easy to spot a style that looks weak on your device. Pick the style that reads well everywhere, not just in the preview. A developer can go one step further. Copy the styled string into a code editor and inspect its length. A styled string may report more characters than the plain version. That extra count comes from combining marks or wide characters. It is normal for some styles. It is worth knowing before the string hits a length limit. The Takeaway for Builders A fancy text generator is a small program with a clear job. It maps plain letters to styled Unicode letters and returns the new string. The Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols block supplies most of the styled sets. The clipboard carries the result because the result is text. No font file travels with it. That simple design is why the tool feels fast. There is no rendering step on the server. There is no image to build. The work is a lookup per character, repeated for a short string. The cost stays tiny even with 36 styles on offer. If you build your own version, start with one style and one table. Test it with real words, not just the alphabet. Check the Script gaps. Check digits and spaces. Check the result on a phone. Once one style is solid, the next 35 are the same pattern with new tables. The charm of the tool is not magic. It is a neat reuse of a Unicode block that was built for math. A generator turns that block into a style picker. You type plain words, and you get styled words back. The words stay words. Only the code points change. Written by Arlo Bennett

title: Brasil lidera registros de vítimas de ransomware na América Latina
author: guiadeti
summary: Brasil lidera os registros de ransomware na América Latina O Brasil liderou a América Latina em publicações de vítimas de ransomware em sites de vazamento de dados. Entre abril e setembro de 2026, a Trellix identificou 102 registros envolvendo organizações brasileiras, contra 56 da Argentina, segunda colocada. Os números fazem parte do Relatório de Ameaças Cibernéticas de novembro de 2026, divulgado pela empresa de segurança digital. No cenário global, o levantamento contabilizou 5.505 publicações de vítimas, atribuídas a 124 grupos criminosos ativos. Segundo a Trellix, esse foi o maior volume registrado em um período de seis meses. A América Latina respondeu por 8,3% das vítimas publicadas no mundo, com Brasil e Argentina nas duas primeiras posições regionais. Rodrigo Buosi, country manager da Trellix no Brasil, classificou a liderança brasileira como um sinal de alerta. Segundo ele, criminosos exploram vulnerabilidades conhecidas, credenciais comprometidas e relações de confiança com fornecedores para invadir organizações. Esses são os caminhos de entrada destacados por Buosi para explicar a exposição das empresas. Campanhas tentam desativar mecanismos de proteção Das 94 campanhas de ransomware analisadas pela Trellix, 40 incluíram tentativas de desativar ou modificar ferramentas de segurança. Em 14 delas, foram identificados recursos voltados a neutralizar soluções de detecção e resposta em endpoints, conhecidas pela sigla EDR, ou a explorar drivers vulneráveis. Essas ações procuram dificultar a identificação da invasão e permitir que os criminosos avancem pelos sistemas comprometidos antes da reação das equipes de segurança. A telemetria da empresa também registrou mais de 2,2 milhões de detecções relacionadas a ransomware em 775 campanhas diferentes, alta de 4,7% em relação ao período anterior. Menções a IA e ataques à cadeia de software aumentam A proporção de campanhas que mencionaram inteligência artificial ou grandes modelos de linguagem, os LLMs, passou de 5,3% para 10,4% no período analisado. Já a participação de ataques à cadeia de suprimentos de software subiu de 9,1% para 11,9%, indicando que essas duas frentes apareceram com maior frequência nas campanhas monitoradas. Nos ataques à cadeia de suprimentos, invasores podem explorar fornecedores, ferramentas de desenvolvimento ou outros componentes usados por várias organizações. O comprometimento de um único elemento pode abrir caminho para atingir diferentes ambientes conectados, segundo a descrição desse tipo de operação no relatório. A Trellix também identificou agentes de IA e malwares autônomos capazes de executar várias etapas de uma invasão com supervisão humana mínima. A empresa descreve essa capacidade como uma evolução em relação ao uso inicial de IA, voltado principalmente à produção de mensagens de phishing. Vulnerabilidades conhecidas continuam entre os alvos, inclusive quando já há correções disponíveis. Como os dados foram reunidos O relatório cobre o período de 1º de abril a 30 de setembro de 2026 e combina dados de telemetria das soluções de segurança da Trellix com informações de fontes abertas e da dark web. Entre os materiais considerados estão publicações em sites que grupos de ransomware usam para divulgar vítimas e ameaçar expor informações. Os números retratam as ameaças identificadas durante esses seis meses. As detecções monitoradas e as publicações em sites de vazamento não confirmam, por si só, infecções nas organizações citadas, e o levantamento não inclui ameaças que escaparam dos mecanismos de identificação. Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/brasil-lidera-publicacoes-vitimas-ransomware-america-latina/

title: Canva ranked first. Why didn't its site appear in that answer's sources?
author: ModelFild
summary: Disclosure: I work on ModelFold GEO, which published the sample report used here. I used AI assistance to draft this article and checked the figures against the public report. This is not a Canva endorsement. Imagine you're auditing AI recommendations for a design tool. You ask, “Which online design tools are best for a small business on a tight budget?” Your brand comes first. Before you call that a win for your website, open the answer's source list. Those are two different results. Read the answer and its sources separately In ModelFold GEO's public Canva sample , measured in English on November 22, 2026 (UTC), Canva had a visibility score of 86/100 , a 90% mention rate , and an average position of 1.5 , across 20 usable answers. The score combines whether the brand shows up and where it ranks. It isn't a click-through rate or a measure of how often Canva's own site was cited. Open the first search result for that small-business question. It lists Canva at #1 , alongside alternatives including Figma, Adobe Express, VistaCreate, and Looka. But the sources shown for that answer don't include canva.com. Zoom out to the full report and the picture changes: the “Most cited sites” table shows adobe.com at 10 , canva.com at 8 , and learn.g2.com at 8 . The official domain does appear elsewhere in the sample. One answer's source list doesn't tell you how the whole set behaves, and a displayed citation doesn't prove which page caused the ranking. Turn that distinction into a repeatable check Write the question a buyer would actually ask. Start with a use case and a constraint, like the budget question above. Leave your brand out of the prompt. Otherwise you're testing what an assistant says about you, not whether it thinks to bring you up. Record the answer and the citations in separate columns. Keep the exact prompt, date, language, brand position (or “not mentioned”), cited URLs, and one sentence describing the answer's rationale if it gives one. Mark your own domain separately. Don't treat a missing link as a missing recommendation. Follow up where a buyer would need better evidence. If an answer mentions your brand but sends readers elsewhere, open the cited pages. Is there a concrete question they answer that your site doesn't? For a budget prompt, that might be a clearly dated comparison of what's available on the free plan. If your site already answers the question well, note that too; a missing citation isn't proof that anything needs fixing. Re-run the same prompts before drawing a conclusion. Compare the rows, not just the headline score. Keep the language and wording fixed for a like-for-like comparison, and treat a change in one answer as something to investigate, not as evidence that an edit worked. Start with one buyer question and two columns: Was the brand recommended? and What pages did the answer cite? The answers can point you to different follow-ups. This dated sample doesn't predict future rankings, guarantee recommendations, or tell you whether anyone clicked.

title: We Tried to Predict the Future of an Ecosystem. Doing Nothing Was a Better Prediction.
author: Emil Fournier
summary: My best friend Timothée and I are working on a project called Arbor. We're trying to find out whether machine learning can predict how ecosystems will evolve over the next ten years. The idea came to us in October after watching a documentary about the Amazon rainforest. We had already been working on AI through GreenTrust AI, but this was a very different problem from anything we had worked on before. Our first experiment We built a small experimental model using historical environmental data to predict environmental conditions one year ahead. One of the most interesting things we found was that our model didn't outperform persistence overall. A persistence model essentially predicts that tomorrow's conditions will be the same as today's. In our case, it assumes that environmental conditions will remain unchanged from one year to the next. Many of the areas we were studying were relatively stable over that period. This meant that a very simple prediction was surprisingly difficult to beat. Our experiment was preliminary, and we're currently working on a more rigorous evaluation. But it made us reconsider parts of our approach. Getting a high overall accuracy doesn't necessarily mean that a model is good at predicting environmental changes. The data problem We're currently working with environmental data from sources such as MapBiomas, SoilGrids and OpenLandMap. One of the difficulties is that these datasets have very different spatial resolutions. Some of the data we want to use have a resolution of around 20–30 meters per pixel, while other datasets have resolutions of approximately 9 km per pixel. Local conditions matter, but so does the environment surrounding an area. We're currently exploring a pyramidal data structure that would allow us to work with information at different spatial resolutions. It's still an early idea, and we haven't yet established whether it will be an effective way to organize our training data. For our first larger study, covering around 10,000 km² in the Brazilian state of Pará, we estimate that we'll need approximately 500–700 GiB of environmental data. What we want to predict Rather than predicting a single environmental indicator, we want to explore whether we can predict changes in several variables related to vegetation, soil, water and fire. I've also been developing a mathematical formula to estimate the ecological condition of an area. Eventually, we want to calculate this score from the variables predicted by our models. Our initial target is to make yearly predictions over ten years. Before getting there, we need to answer a few questions: Can deep learning outperform persistence and other simpler models? How well can a model trained in one geographical area generalize to another? Which environmental variables can actually be predicted reliably? How should we estimate and communicate uncertainty? We're considering Markov models, naive Bayes classifiers and persistence models as baselines, depending on the prediction task. We're also interested in evaluating performance separately on stable areas and areas that have actually undergone environmental changes. What's next for Arbor? One of our biggest limitations right now is access to computing resources. We're developing Arbor ourselves, but running larger experiments and properly evaluating our models requires funding. We've launched a campaign on Manifund to help cover these costs. Our funding goal ranges from $500 for smaller experiments to $44,000 for our full research program. If you're interested in the project, our research proposal and funding breakdown are available here: Arbor – Using AI to Restore Nature Worldwide We're also interested in hearing from developers and researchers who have experience with geospatial machine learning or environmental forecasting. Where we're going with this The long-term idea behind Arbor is to help people working in ecological restoration better understand how an ecosystem might evolve before deciding how to intervene. We're not at the point where we can recommend restoration strategies. Predicting environmental changes is already a difficult problem, and predicting the effects of human interventions introduces another set of challenges. Timothée and I are both 17, and we're developing Arbor alongside our studies in Switzerland. We're currently preparing our first research report, which we hope to finish by December 12. We plan to publish our methodology, benchmarks, computational estimates and limitations. I'd be particularly interested in hearing from people who have worked with geospatial machine learning, multiresolution raster data or long-term environmental forecasting. How would you approach the data structure? Which baselines would you use? How would you evaluate a model when most of the observed environment remains stable? I'd love to hear your thoughts.

title: How to Audit a Lean Proof Artifact Before You Trust It
author: RobustTrueTry
summary: A Lean 4 repository that claims to prove the Riemann Hypothesis surfaced recently. The machine checks pass. That is not the same thing as a proof you can trust, and knowing the difference matters for any artifact you might depend on. By the end you will know how to pin a Lean toolchain, check which axioms a theorem actually uses, and spot the gaps a compiler cannot catch. Machine check versus mathematical review A proof assistant like Lean checks every inference step against its kernel. If lake build succeeds, no step is invalid. That guarantee is real and strong. What it does not cover: Whether the theorem statements say what the authors think they say Whether any axiom sneaks in assumptions the community rejects Whether anyone has actually read the argument The GRH artifact is explicit about this: it has passed machine checks only, with no mathematician reading it through and no accompanying paper. Treat that status as the baseline for any research repo you encounter. Pin the exact toolchain first Lean proofs are fragile across versions. Mathlib changes daily, and lemma names move. An artifact pinned to Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib commit 56a00585 will often fail to build against today's Mathlib. Use the versions the artifact declares, not whatever is current: # inside the project folder eLNTOOLCHAIN = leanprover/lean4:v4.35.0 eLAKE exe cache get # fetches prebuilt Mathlib olean files eLAKE build (Replace the leading e with nothing — those are elan -managed, so install elan first and the toolchain file in the repo will select the right Lean automatically.) The cache get step matters most. Building Mathlib from source takes hours; downloading cached binaries takes minutes. On a 12-core machine with 24 GB of RAM, expect roughly an hour for the artifact itself, more if the cache step is skipped or fails. Check the axioms This is the step most people skip and the one that carries the most information. Lean's kernel tracks every axiom a theorem depends on. Standard Mathlib work uses three: propext (propositional extensionality), Classical.choice (classical logic), and Quot.sound (quotient types). Anything beyond those deserves scrutiny — in particular, a proof that lists sorryAx is not a proof at all. A tiny script prints the dependency set: import GRH open Lean def main : IO Unit := do let env ← importModules # [ { module := `GRH}] {} for (name, info) in env.constants.toList do if let some ax := info.axiomArg? then IO.println s"{name}: {ax}" In practice, run the artifact's own script: lake env lean scripts/PrintAxioms.lean Then read the output. Three axioms is a clean result. If you see sorryAx , the artifact contains an admitted gap regardless of what the README claims. Read the theorem statements, not the proofs The kernel verified some statement. Your job is to confirm it is the statement you care about. Find the top-level theorem declarations and read them. What to look for Definitions : does DirichletL match the series and functional equation you expect? A nonstandard definition can make a false claim trivially true. Implicit arguments : Lean infers many arguments silently. An implicit that should be explicit can weaken the statement. Universe and type assumptions : check that the theorem is not stated in a degenerate type where it holds vacuously. For the GRH artifact specifically, the readable edition starts at grh/GUIDE.md — a curated entry path is a good sign, but it is still on you to confirm the final statements. Two editions, one claim of equivalence The artifact ships two versions: a readable edition around 300,000 lines and a compact edition around 76,000. Both claim to prove the same five theorems. Nothing in the build process enforces that the two are equivalent. A skeptical audit checks that each edition's target theorems have the same statement — types you can diff by eye — even if the proofs differ completely. Statement-level agreement plus independent axiom checks give you far more confidence than either edition alone. Check What it catches Effort lake build Invalid inference steps Low — run it Axiom report Hidden assumptions, sorryAx Low — run it Statement review Vacuous or nonstandard claims Medium — read the final theorems Two-edition diff Statement drift between versions Medium Full human review Everything above Infeasible for most What can still go wrong Kernel-level validity is the floor, not the ceiling. Statements can be subtly weaker than intended. Definitions can diverge from convention in ways that are legal but misleading. And a result nobody has read has no social correction mechanism: if a definition is wrong, no issue tracker comment will tell you, because the repository explicitly does not accept contributions. For production work the rule is simple. You may cite a machine-checked result with the exact version, commit, and axiom report. You should not build on one without reading its final statements yourself. Key takeaways A successful lake build proves every step is valid, but says nothing about whether the theorem statements mean what you assume. Always run an axiom report and reject any artifact whose dependencies extend beyond propext , Classical.choice , and Quot.sound without justification; sorryAx means the proof is incomplete. Pin Lean and Mathlib versions exactly — Mathlib moves daily and unpinned builds usually fail. Read the top-level theorem statements and their definitions; this is where false claims hide in valid proofs. Source GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, in Lean 4 — I added the practical audit workflow the README omits: toolchain pinning, axiom checking, statement review, and the two-edition comparison. title: TaskCarry: project memory for work across AI chats
author: TaskCarry
summary: I’m building TaskCarry because using more AI chats shouldn’t mean doing more handoffs yourself. One chat updates a draft. A teammate reviews another version. Days later, you’re digging through conversations to work out what was actually approved. TaskCarry is an open-source project memory and collaboration toolkit. It connects decisions, work and next steps across AI chats and teammates into one lasting project record. Which version did we actually agree on? Engineering finishes a change. Someone else reviews it. A third person continues the project later. The useful handoff is more than “done”: the work, the review, and the version the team accepted need to stay connected. TaskCarry gives collaborators a saved project record to return to instead of piecing together scattered chats. We solved this before. Where did that experience go? A useful method shouldn’t disappear when you switch chats or collaborators. Keep the earlier solution with the project so the next collaborator can find what worked and decide whether it fits the current task. Bring AI together. Keep projects moving. Explore the source and getting-started guide: bryan123466/taskcarry on GitHub . What gets lost most often in your AI workflow: the agreed version, the reasoning, or the next step? Prepared with AI assistance and the project owner’s editorial direction.
